svg.aria-label: The three parts of a Cognito ID token, its claims, and the verification check each claim supports
svg.title: Anatomy of a Strobe ID token — and what each check proves
svg.text: Anatomy of a Strobe ID token — and what each check proves
A JWT is three base64url parts joined by dots. Anyone can read the first two; only the third makes them trustworthy. Values below are illustrative.
ENCODED (what travels in authenticate._meta.idToken and in Authorization: Bearer …)
WHAT THE VERIFIER CHECKS (aws-jwt-verify in the agent · FastMCP JWTVerifier · API Gateway authorizer)
Which public key should I use?
Pick the matching key from the pool's JWKS
The user's permanent id; becomes userId in every filter
Did OUR user pool issue it?
Must equal the pool URL built from the SSM pool id
Was it minted for OUR app?
other app client, or an access token → reject
Is it the right kind of token?
Was it signed by Cognito, unedited?
Verify RS256 with the kid's public key
Anyone holding the token can read the payload — the WebUI decodes it
itself just to show your name (tokenLabel() in main.ts). So: never put
secrets in claims, and never trust a claim until the signature checks out.
…and why it never goes in a URL
A ?id_token= query string lands in ALB access logs and browser history,
where it is readable — and usable until exp. Strobe sends it inside the
Why Strobe uses the ID token, not the access token
Both the agent and the MCP server check aud, so an access token would be rejected by design.
